Exploit Season: Past the Bear, Not Yet Bull — and the Hackers Are Working Overtime

by IbenPharmin

The bear market is behind us. The bull hasn't actually shown up. And in the in-between, crypto is bleeding — $2.8 billion to exploits this year, the cadence still climbing, and now both sides of the war are running AI.

Here's my read on where this market actually is: we're past the bear. The forced sellers are gone, the tourists are gone, the contagion is gone. But nobody serious is calling this a bull market either — no euphoria, no mania, no Uber driver asking about memecoins. We're in the hallway between regimes.

And hallways are where people get robbed.

Because while price chops sideways waiting for a regime, something else has been running all year with zero chop at all: the exploits. Not one big headline hack — a cadence. A string of them, going back months, arriving faster, and increasingly built with the same AI tools the rest of us use to write tweets. This is exploit season. Let me show you the tape.

The tape: six months of bleeding

CertiK's running count for 2026, as of mid-October: $2.81 billion stolen across 693 incidents. About $452 million of that has been frozen or returned, which softens the net to roughly $2.35 billion — "softens" doing a lot of work in that sentence. (🔗 CertiK via CryptoSlate)

The year didn't start hot. It built.

April was the early warning. On April 1, Drift Protocol on Solana lost about $285 million — an exploit investigators attributed to North Korea. Seventeen days later, KelpDAO lost roughly $291 million through a compromised LayerZero bridge checker; LayerZero publicly pointed at the Lazarus Group. April closed at $646.9 million in total losses. (🔗 CertiK, PeckShield)

July printed $210 million, and quietly produced the year's most important footnote: Sysdig described JADEPUFFER, which it called the first known ransomware attack carried out by an AI agent with no human in control. Hold that thought. (🔗 PeckShield; The Decoder)

August is where the frequency story shows up. Losses actually fell to $136.3 million — but the incident count hit 50 major hacks, the most of any month all year to that point, and the average haul shrank to about $2.7 million. Read that again: more attacks, smaller scores. That's not a burglar. That's an assembly line. (🔗 PeckShield via BeInCrypto)

September was the worst month of 2026. PeckShield counted 55 major incidents and $766.5 million stolen; CertiK counted 97 incidents at $768.4 million — a ~462% jump from August. Two hits did most of the damage. On September 6, attackers pulled roughly 4,000 BTC — about $320 million — out of the Liquid Network's federation wallet; Blockstream attributed it to a bug in Elements, the software Liquid runs on, and purported white-hats later returned 3,400 BTC, worth around $270 million. On September 24, Bitget lost about $388 million — the year's biggest single theft — after, per CEO Gracy Chen, a flaw in a third-party security product handed the attacker high-level internal credentials used to issue fraudulent withdrawals. Chen said private keys were never compromised and cold storage was untouched; SlowMist later traced the intrusion to an August 31 zero-day, and Elliptic says North Korean involvement is "highly probable." Bitget says its user protection fund — over $464 million — covers the loss, and CEO Gracy Chen said in an October 24 interview that users suffered no losses and the fund has been replenished from company capital. (🔗 Cointelegraph, CoinMarketCap, Decrypt, TokenPost)

And October hasn't slowed down. On October 17, an attacker forged a mint message through Cysic's cross-chain bridge, created 10 million unauthorized CYS, dumped 7.2 million of them inside half an hour, and bridged about $727,000 to Ethereum — before Cysic's blacklist landed 76 minutes after the mint. By October 23, PeckShield had tied a ~$744,000 Tornado Cash deposit to that same attacker — and the timing is the punchline. The deposit landed after Cysic offered a 10% bounty: return 275.872 ETH (about $665,000) and keep the rest. The attacker answered by sending 300 ETH and 30.4 BNB (about $744,000) into Tornado Cash instead, leaving roughly $45 in the wallet. So much for the bounty. (🔗 Cointelegraph, Cryptopolitan)

Six months. Every month, another entry. That's not a crime wave, it's a season.

The accelerant: bug-hunting got cheap

So why now? Part of it is the in-between market itself — less euphoria means less scrutiny, thinner teams, protocols running on fumes. But the bigger accelerant is the one nobody in this industry can un-invent: modern AI models have collapsed the cost of finding and weaponizing bugs.

Don't take my word for it. Take Bitcoin Core's.

On October 22, Bitcoin Core merged a change to its security policy, proposed by contributor Antoine Poinsot. The old system embargoed medium and high-severity bugs for up to a year while fixes quietly shipped. The new policy creates a class called "easily discoverable" — defined as vulnerabilities that can be found "with minimal effort, such as through a simple LLM prompt" — and those now get point-release fixes for every maintained version as soon as possible, embargo be damned. Poinsot's reasoning, in his own words: "We recently experienced an increase in the number of reports for security vulnerabilities that can be easily (re-)discovered. This is largely due to LLMs drastically reducing the bar to find certain classes of issues." (🔗 Bitcoin Magazine, Unchained)

Sit with that. The most conservative engineering culture in crypto just rewrote a decade of disclosure doctrine because secrecy stopped working. If a bug is one prompt away, the only defense left is patch speed.

And the offensive side is already agent-shaped. On October 21, Symantec's Threat Hunter Team published its analysis of an autonomous agent — captured by an AI honeypot over the summer — built to hunt the internet for exposed LLM endpoints and hijack them. One directive, literally named "Skynet mode," runs a loop: scan for targets, infect them, deploy cryptominers, reinfect — for up to 100,000 steps without asking a human anything. The agent carried around 74 offensive tool definitions, and the victim's model pays the compute bill. The honeypot logged over 127,000 external requests from tens of thousands of addresses probing for exactly this kind of opening. (🔗 Symantec via Security.com)

CZ made the retail version of the same point on October 23: AI doesn't need to crack Bitcoin's encryption — banks and the internet run weaker encryption anyway — because leaked data plus AI-polished phishing and social engineering is already the real danger. "Stay SAFU," as the man says. Contrast that with Ethereum researcher Justin Drake, who on October 7 urged the industry to "calmly start planning for 'bunker mode'" against AI breaking wallet math. Two heavyweight reads, same conclusion from opposite directions: the models changed the threat model. (🔗 BeInCrypto)

The defense runs on models too

Here's the part that keeps this from being pure doom: the defense has gone AI-native just as fast.

Binance reports that in the first half of 2026, its AI security stack prevented approximately $4.6 billion in potential losses and protected over 8 million users. The numbers underneath: more than 100 AI models making 80–90% of real-time risk decisions, over 42,000 malicious addresses blacklisted, more than 14,000 real-time warnings issued per day. Those are Binance's own figures — "potential losses prevented" is an estimate, not recovered cash — but even discounted, the shape of it is the story. (🔗 PR Newswire)

Add Bitcoin Core's answer — patch speed over secrecy — and Liquid's 3,400 BTC coming home, and the pattern is clear: offense and defense both run on models now. The war isn't hackers vs. protocols anymore. It's model vs. model, at machine speed, with your funds on the field.

Exhibit A: Initia

Which brings us to this week. October 23, 15:41 UTC: Initia halted its Layer 1 and every rollup on top of it after a security incident. Co-founder Ezaan Mangalji said preliminary findings point to a previously unknown "Day 0" bug in the network's MoveVM implementation that allowed unauthorized token minting — and that the attacker minted and bridged out roughly $2.7 million in AUSD, ETH, and USDC before the pause. Researcher Spreek put the cashed-out figure at about $2.6 million and flagged more funds in transit. Initia itself has not confirmed a final figure — and as of October 27, the chain is still halted and no post-mortem is out — but Initia has now posted that a remediation plan is drafted and in audit by security partners, with backing restoration and an orderly L1 + rollup restart expected in the coming days once the audit completes; no specific restart date has been announced yet. Upbit froze INIT deposits and withdrawals within sixteen minutes of the halt; Bithumb froze them too and issued an investment warning, and KuCoin followed on October 24. On October 28, the Initia Foundation approved funding to restore 1:1 backing for iUSD collateral — capped at 1.08 million USDC, 105 ETH, and 1.4 million AUSD0, with transfers subject to reconciliation and final approval, and backing restored when the chain resumes. On October 26, Upbit and Bithumb designated INIT a trading-caution asset under Korea's Virtual Asset User Protection Act; deposits and withdrawals remain suspended, spot trading continues, with a review window of November 23–27. (🔗 TokenPost, BlockchainReporter) One wrinkle worth noting: Agora, the AUSD issuer, disputes the AUSD half of the story — it says no AUSD contract is deployed on Initia and no AUSD was minted there, and that the 1.4 million AUSD that moved was existing tokens leaving a LayerZero adapter, later swapped for about 581 ETH. The total estimates stay preliminary either way. INIT dumped 14% on the news — then reversed to trade up 14% on the day, because of course it did. This market is feral. (🔗 The Block, PANews, Unchained, Cointelegraph)

A chain halted. Two major exchanges freezing transfers. A mint bug, bridged out in minutes. Six days after Cysic. Two days after the Skynet report. One day after Bitcoin Core admitted the prompt is mightier than the embargo.

Season's still open.

And it didn't pause for the weekend. On October 24, Ethereum project X100 lost control of its on-chain governance after attackers used a flash loan to buy their way into two of its three "Senate" seats — then used that majority to drain treasury tokens and liquidity, realizing roughly $4.85 million in USDT, with the X token crashing 96%. Blockaid flagged the attack as still in progress. The design flaws are almost boring in how avoidable they read: instant voting with no snapshots, proposals executable immediately, no timelocks, no minimum holding periods. Different vector, same season. (🔗 CryptoTimes, Blockaid)

The verdict

My thesis, straight: we're past the bear and not yet in a bull, and the defining meta of this in-between market isn't a narrative coin or a sector rotation — it's security. $2.8 billion gone in ten months. Incident counts tripling from January (16 major hacks) to September (55). Average hauls shrinking while frequency climbs — that's industrialization, and the AI accelerant works on both ends of it.

In a bull market, the chart forgives sloppy security. In a bear market, there's nothing left to steal. In this market — real money sitting in protocols, attention elsewhere — a project's security posture isn't a footnote in the docs. It's part of the fundamentals, same as tokenomics or treasury. The teams treating it that way are the ones whose chains won't be the next exhibit.

Now you tell me

Are we actually in "exploit season," or is this just what crypto looks like now — permanently, a background tax on everything built here? And the real question: when the bull does show up and the tourists return with fresh money, does the cadence get worse? Tell me where I'm wrong.
